# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical Reading: Varga & Holm Comment on the Halden Pilot

This comment has two parts that deserve very different levels of confidence.

- **Sections 1–5** are a valuable data-based re-analysis. They confirm, with microdata, most of the concerns raised about the Halden working paper.
- **Sections 6–8** go well beyond that evidence. The conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" isn't supported by the authors' own corrected numbers. It is contradicted by the Varden trial, which the comment cites selectively.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are correct:
- **Table 2:** 95.1 / 0.8 gives +18.9%, 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%, and 95.4 / 0.861 gives +10.8%.
- **Hours:** 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%, and 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 gives −2.6%.

Two items don't add up.

**1. The hours decomposition is inconsistent with the totals.**

| Component | Hours per week |
|---|---|
| Scheduled | 32 |
| Longer days (+0.7 h × 4 days) | +2.8 |
| Logged work on the day off | +1.6 |
| **Implied actual hours** | **≈ 36.4** |
| Reported actual hours | 34.6 |

Measuring the +0.7 against baseline actual days (8.06 h) makes the gap larger, not smaller. Either the components or the total is wrong. The 14.1% figure feeds directly into Table 2.

**2. The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated.** A linear decline from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 SD at month 6 reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten". This is minor, but it sits in the paper's most speculative argument.

## What the comment does well

**Attrition (§1).** This is the most important new fact. The Halden paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata show:
- seven of the nine withdrew after the schedule started;
- six of the nine cited workload or inability to maintain output.

That is a misdescription in the original paper, not just a limitation. It turns survivorship bias from a possibility into a documented problem.

**Output measure (§2).** Managers' indices exceeded the record-based indices in 19 of 23 organisations. That is direct evidence of the optimistic-rater bias that could previously only be suspected.

**Hours (§3).** Logged actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. The authors also note that unlogged work would push the true figure lower still. This matches Varden's finding of −13% in case-processing offices.

**Revenue and sector claims (§4–5).** These are correct and well documented. The three retail organisations with records show an 11.2% output fall. That closely matches Varden's −11.4% in counter offices, though n = 3 is very small.

**Data note.** The authors are candid that the corrections apply to non-random subsets.

## Problems in the re-analysis itself

**1. The abstract overstates what was corrected.** It says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. The first problem is attrition, and Table 2 doesn't correct for it at all. Only output and hours are corrected. Attrition is described but never quantified.

The authors could have bounded its effect. For example, they could assume the nine withdrawals had zero or negative per-hour gains and see how much the mean moves.

**2. Table 2 mixes corrections with changing samples.** Its rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. Differences between rows therefore combine the effect of each correction with differences between subsets. A cleaner decomposition would apply all four specifications to the same 17 organisations.

**3. There is no uncertainty anywhere.** No row of Table 2 has a confidence interval. An estimate from 17 self-selected organisations could be quite imprecise.

**4. Records are treated as ground truth without argument.** Some record measures are narrow, such as tickets closed. One is "billable hours delivered", which is itself a measure of hours. For that measure, "output per hour" is essentially a utilisation rate. Manager indices are clearly biased upward, but records may be biased downward or measure something different.

## Where the argument outruns the evidence

**1. "Most" becomes "entirely" without new evidence.** The abstract says the four problems account for "most" of the gain. The conclusion says the gains are "entirely an artifact". The only bridge between the two is the novelty argument in §6, which is conjecture. The authors' own best estimate is still +10.8%, not zero.

**2. The novelty argument has the wrong outcome and the wrong method.**
- **It tracks energy, not output.** Self-reported energy is a mood measure. Nothing shows that output followed it.
- **It extrapolates linearly from two points.** Energy could just as plausibly level off at a positive value.
- **It skips the direct test.** Halden collected the output index monthly, and the authors have the microdata. They could have checked whether output per hour declined from month 3 to month 6. That test is the obvious one, and its absence is conspicuous.
- **It applies the burden of proof unevenly.** It's fair to say a durable effect isn't proven. But "entirely an artifact" is also a positive claim, and it isn't proven either.

**3. Varden is cited selectively.** The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". The same randomised trial, using record-based output and timesheet hours, also found:
- output per actual hour up **12.5% (95% CI 6.9 to 18.4)** in case-processing offices;
- output per employee essentially unchanged in those offices.

That design removes self-selection, manager bias and the scheduled-hours error. Those are the comment's main proposed artifacts. Novelty isn't excluded, since Varden staff knew their assignment, but Varden ran for nine months rather than six.

Notably, the comment's corrected Halden estimate (+10.8%) is very close to Varden's randomised estimate (+12.5%). That convergence is evidence for a real, moderate per-hour gain in backlog-type work, and the comment never mentions it.

**4. The meetings critique mischaracterises the Varden analysis.**
- **The offices weren't a post hoc subgroup.** The seven treated case-processing offices are a pre-specified randomisation stratum. The analysis was unregistered, but the group was fixed in advance.
- **The data weren't collected after the results were known.** Meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month outcomes existed.
- **Varden already made the same caveats.** Its authors said a seven-office correlation can't establish a mechanism, and they registered a confirmatory test. The comment attacks a claim they didn't make.
- **Corroborating evidence is ignored.** In the Halden interviews, 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings.

The meetings account is the main alternative to "artifact". If it holds, it implies a real productivity gain from removing low-value time. Dismissing it sweepingly is convenient for the conclusion.

**5. The generalisation is too broad.** One flawed pilot doesn't justify a verdict on "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general.

## Synthesis across the three documents

| Question | Halden claim | Varden (randomised) | Varga & Holm | Best current reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, backlog or knowledge work | +23.4% | +12.5% (CI 6.9 to 18.4) | +10.8% after corrections, then "zero" | **Roughly 10–13%**, consistent across two very different designs. Durability unknown. |
| Output per employee, backlog work | ~−1% (manager-rated) | −2.1% (CI −6.8 to +2.6) | ~−5% (records) | Small loss, likely 0–7% |
| Coverage-bound work | Sector-general gains | Output −11.4%, worse service | Output −11.2% (n = 3) | **Clear output loss.** All three sources agree. |
| Scheduled vs actual hours | Assumed −20% | −13% to −17% | −14% (decomposition inconsistent) | Actual reduction about 13–17% |
| Mechanism | Fatigue | Meetings, exploratory | Novelty | **Unresolved.** Meetings is suggestive, novelty is untested. |
| Durability | Not addressed | 24-month follow-up under way | Presumed to fade | **Open question.** The Varden follow-up and Halden's monthly output data are the key tests. |

## Bottom line

The comment shows that the Halden headline was inflated by about half, and that Halden misreported its attrition. Both are important contributions.

Its own conclusion is weaker than its evidence. The corrected Halden estimate and the randomised Varden estimate converge on a moderate per-hour gain in backlog-type work. They also agree on output losses where work depends on presence. Whether the gain lasts is the genuine open question, and nothing in this comment answers it.
